aliases: the real cost of a choice
concept: The real cost of a choice is what you give up for it: the value of your next-best option, minus what that option would have cost you. Money already spent and gone doesn't count.

misconceptions.label: Free means it costs nothing
misconceptions.why_tempting: No money leaves your pocket, so it feels free.
misconceptions.refutation: Going uses up the evening you could have spent on your next-best option. What that option was worth to you, minus its price, is the cost.
misconceptions.source_note: Quotes Ferraro & Taylor's (2005) Clapton/Dylan question; only 21.6% of economists surveyed picked the right answer ($10)

misconceptions.label: The cost is the other option's price tag
misconceptions.why_tempting: The $40 price is the only cost you can see written down.
misconceptions.refutation: Skipping the other show also saves you its $40 price. You give up $50 of enjoyment but keep $40, so you lose $10 of value.
misconceptions.source_note: Ferraro & Taylor question as quoted: 'The correct answer is (b), the net value to you of buying a ticket and attending the Dylan concert'

misconceptions.label: The cost is the full value of what I skip
misconceptions.why_tempting: You'd enjoy the other show $50 worth, so giving it up feels like losing $50.
misconceptions.refutation: You'd have paid $40 to get that $50 of enjoyment, so the net you give up is $50 - $40 = $10.
misconceptions.source_note: Ferraro & Taylor: the right answer is the net value, $50 - $40 = $10

misconceptions.label: Only cash you pay counts as cost
misconceptions.why_tempting: Bills and prices are visible; pay you never receive leaves no trace.
misconceptions.refutation: Income or time you give up is a real cost too, even though no bill arrives.
misconceptions.source_note: 'opportunity costs are not restricted to monetary or financial costs: the real cost of output forgone, lost time... should also be considered'

misconceptions.label: Money already spent should steer the choice
misconceptions.why_tempting: Skipping something you paid for feels like throwing the money away.
misconceptions.refutation: The money is gone whether you go or not, so it can't help you choose. Only what's ahead counts: which evening would you enjoy more?
misconceptions.source_note: Sunk cost fallacy: 'a greater tendency to continue an endeavor once an investment in money, effort, or time has been made'

items.prompt: You win a free concert ticket for tonight (you can't sell it). Your next-best plan is another show: tickets cost $40, and you'd happily pay up to $50 to go. What do you give up by going to the free concert (its opportunity cost)?

options.text: $50: what the other show is worth to me

steps: Going to the free concert means skipping the other show.
The other show would give you $50 worth of enjoyment...
...but you'd have to pay $40 for it, money you keep by skipping.
So you give up $50 - $40 = $10 of value: that's the opportunity cost.

items.prompt: A student pays $20,000 a year in tuition. Instead of studying, she could work full time and earn $30,000 a year. Her rent and food cost the same either way. What does a year of college really cost her?

options.text: $50,000: tuition plus the pay she gives up

items.prompt: You paid $60 for a concert ticket you can't refund or sell. On the night, you're tired and would honestly enjoy staying home more. Should the $60 you already paid push you toward going?

options.text: No: the $60 is gone either way, so pick the evening you'd enjoy more

steps: If you go: the $60 is spent, and you get an evening you'd enjoy less.
If you stay home: the $60 is spent, and you get the evening you'd enjoy more.
The $60 is the same in both futures, so it can't tip the choice.
Going 'so it isn't wasted' just adds a worse evening to the lost money.
